headline: South Africa's ruling party loses ground in local votes

sources.title: South Africa's ANC suffers setback in local elections (Al Jazeera, AFP and Reuters)

chunks.text: South Africans voted in local elections on November 4, 2026. These elections choose the [[councils]] that run cities and towns. As results {{came in}}, they showed a [[sharp drop]] for the African National Congress. This party led the fight against [[apartheid]], the old system of [[white minority rule]]. It has led the national government since 1994. In the final results, announced on November 8, it had 30.8 percent of the vote, down from 45.6 percent in 2021.

verbs.why: Test results usually come in after a few days. Orders come in fast in December. As results came in, they showed a sharp drop for the African National Congress.

chunks.text: Analysts say many voters have {{turned away from}} the party over crime, [[corruption]], [[a lack of jobs]] and poor [[public services]]. In Johannesburg, the biggest city, homes are often {{cut off}} from water and power. Trash {{piles up}} on the streets, and roads are full of [[potholes]]. The city has had 10 mayors in about 10 years under [[shaky]] [[coalitions]], groups of parties that govern together.

verbs.wrong: To move to a different city
verbs.why: Fans often turn away from a band after a bad album. Shoppers turn away from a store when its prices rise. Analysts say many voters have turned away from the party.

verbs.correct: To stop the supply of something
verbs.wrong: To raise the price of something
verbs.why: The power company cuts off service when people do not pay the bill. Big storms often cut off power in our area. In Johannesburg, homes are often cut off from water and power.

verbs.correct: To grow larger as more is added
verbs.wrong: To be burned in the open air
verbs.why: Dirty dishes pile up when I am busy. Bills pile up fast when you lose your job. In Johannesburg, trash piles up on the streets.

chunks.text: The [[pro-business]] Democratic Alliance came second, with 24.6 percent. It {{pulled ahead}} in Johannesburg, with about 35 percent. It {{held on to}} Cape Town, which it has run since 2006. A party led by former president Jacob Zuma came third, with about 10 percent. It {{broke away}} from the African National Congress in 2023. It came first in Durban, a [[port city]]. [[Turnout]], the share of [[registered voters]] who voted, {{went up}} from 45.9 percent to 52 percent, the election commission said.

verbs.correct: To take the lead in a race
verbs.wrong: To give up and leave a race
verbs.why: Our team often pulls ahead in the second half. The fastest runner pulls ahead after the first mile. The Democratic Alliance pulled ahead in Johannesburg, with about 35 percent.

verbs.wrong: To sell something to a company
verbs.why: Strong teams hold on to the lead until the final minute. Many families hold on to their land for generations. The Democratic Alliance held on to Cape Town, which it has run since 2006.

verbs.correct: To leave a group and form a new one
verbs.wrong: To lose an election by a lot
verbs.why: Sometimes a few members break away and start their own club. Small groups often break away from large unions. A party led by former president Jacob Zuma broke away from the African National Congress in 2023.
Prices go up every winter. Rent goes up almost every year in big cities. Turnout went up from 45.9 percent in 2021 to 52 percent.

chunks.text: An analyst at a research company said the higher turnout [[suggests]] that supporters of the African National Congress did not {{stay away}}. Instead, they {{showed up}} and chose other parties. The commission called the vote free and fair. In 127 councils, including Johannesburg's, no party won a [[majority]], or more than half of the [[seats]]. Parties have two weeks to {{team up}} and choose mayors. The ruling party could still {{end up}} leading some cities.

verbs.correct: To choose not to be present
verbs.wrong: To cheat in a vote count
verbs.why: Many fans stay away when ticket prices are too high. Some parents stay away from school meetings because of work. An analyst said supporters of the African National Congress did not stay away.

verbs.correct: To be present and take part
verbs.wrong: To count the votes by hand
verbs.why: Most of my friends show up for my birthday party. Only a few people show up when it rains. Instead of staying home, its supporters showed up and chose other parties.

verbs.correct: To work as one group for a goal
verbs.wrong: To argue in a public meeting
verbs.why: Two small shops team up to sell their goods online. Neighbors often team up to clean the local park. Parties have two weeks to team up and choose mayors.

verbs.correct: To finally be in a certain situation
verbs.wrong: To lose control of a city council
verbs.why: People who miss the bus often end up walking to work. Many students end up working in a field they never planned. The African National Congress could still end up leading some cities.

mainIdea.s: Final results in South Africa's local elections show support for the African National Congress falling hard. Analysts say voters are angry about crime, jobs and poor water and power service.
mainIdea.why: In the final results, the party had 30.8 percent, down from 45.6 percent. Analysts say many voters have turned away from it over crime, jobs and services.

mainIdea.s: South Africa's oldest party lost many seats because far fewer people voted in the local elections. Many of its usual supporters stayed home, so rivals easily won Johannesburg and Durban.
mainIdea.why: Close, but turnout went up from 45.9 percent to 52 percent. An analyst said the party's supporters showed up and chose other parties.

mainIdea.s: South Africans chose a new president in a national vote held on a rainy Wednesday in November. The winner has promised to build new homes and repair roads in every province by 2029.
mainIdea.why: This story is about local elections for city and town councils. The final results showed a sharp drop for the African National Congress.

tf.s: Analysts say many voters have turned away from the African National Congress.
tf.why: Voters are unhappy about crime, corruption, a lack of jobs and poor public services.

tf.s: In Johannesburg, homes are rarely cut off from water and power.
tf.why: Homes there are often cut off from water and power, and trash piles up on the streets.

tf.s: The Democratic Alliance pulled ahead in Johannesburg.
tf.why: The pro-business party won about 35 percent there and came second nationally.

tf.s: Fewer South Africans showed up to vote than in 2021.
tf.why: Turnout went up. An analyst said the party's supporters showed up but chose other parties.

tf.s: A party led by former president Jacob Zuma broke away from the ruling party.
tf.why: The party broke away in 2023, came third nationally and came first in Durban.

tf.s: The African National Congress won more than half of the vote.
tf.why: As the final results came in, it had about 31 percent, far less than half.

lines.text: Did you see the local election results from South Africa?
A little. The ANC, the African National Congress, did badly, right?
Very badly. When the final results {{came in}} on November 8, it had only about 31 percent of the vote.
Wow. It won more than 45 percent in 2021. That's [[a big blow]].
Analysts say a lot of voters have {{turned away from}} the party.
Why? What are people upset about?
Crime, jobs and basic services. In Johannesburg, homes get {{cut off}} from water and power all the time.
And I read that trash {{piles up}} on the streets. People have [[had enough]].
Right. The Democratic Alliance {{pulled ahead}} there, and it {{held on to}} Cape Town.
It {{broke away}} from the ANC in 2023. It came third overall, but it finished first in Durban.
Did fewer people vote this time?
No, turnout {{went up}}. One analyst said ANC voters didn't {{stay away}}. They {{showed up}} and picked other parties.
So people still wanted to vote. They just felt it was [[time for a change]].
I think so. In a lot of cities, no party has a majority, so parties have two weeks to {{team up}}.
Maybe. The final count is done, but the party could still {{end up}} leading some city governments.

expressions.def: Used to say that someone is tired of a bad situation and wants it to stop
ex: I'd had enough of the noise by midnight.

expressions.def: Used to say that people want something new or different now
ex: After ten years in the same job, she felt it was time for a change.

expressions.def: Used to say that a situation is starting to change in a clear way
ex: After three losses in a row, the tide is turning for our team.
